summary:
Campeche stands under Mexico's national framework for legal gender recognition, which remains incomplete. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of Mexico's 32 states now operate an administrative procedure for recognising a person's gender in official documents, and called on the states that lack such procedures to adopt them. The same dispatch warned that implementation differs sharply from one state to another, and that where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

Campeche's elected congress passed a 2024 reform to the Civil Code creating an administrative legal gender recognition procedure. A trans visitor or resident can therefore have identity documents aligned through an administrative route rather than through litigation, which is the single most consequential legal fact for anyone crossing borders or dealing with police, banking and health services on mismatched documents.

Formal rights and their enforcement diverge. Analysis published by Caroline Beer on the LSE USAPP blog (22 November 2024) found that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are rarely enjoyed in practice. Beer stated explicitly that her earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ people in Mexico are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

Delays and refusals in name and gender recognition in the neighbouring state of Tabasco leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying everyday discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police, the Human Rights Watch report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024) found. That report set these findings against killings including a trans woman found dead in the Carrizal River in August 2023.

Killings of trans people continue and have drawn public protest. The Associated Press reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening period of that year, including activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, which triggered LGBTQ+ outrage and street demonstrations. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that violence against trans people and the murder of LGBTI+ defenders had increased over the previous year. Transgender Europe monitoring recorded 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico from 2008 to September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a total second only to Brazil's 100.

Mexico City's congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide with up to 70 years' imprisonment, making it the second of Mexico's 32 states to do so. The law is named for Paola Buenrostro, a trans sex worker murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished; activists quoted at the time described the measure as critical to their feeling safe in the capital. It obliges the attorney-general's office to publish statistics on crimes against the LGBTQ+ community.

Regional oversight bodies have pressed the authorities. In 2024 the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded investigation of all LGBTI violations using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may reach alarming levels.
tangentialFactors:
Criminalisation of transfemicide remains exceptional rather than general. When Mexico City's congress adopted the Paola Buenrostro law in July 2024 it became only the second of Mexico's 32 states to create such an offence, which indicates that Campeche had no transfemicide-specific provision in its penal code at that date and that a trans killing there would be prosecuted under ordinary homicide provisions.

The scale of lethal violence against trans people in Mexico is documented nationally rather than by state. Transgender Europe counted 593 transfeminicidios between 2008 and September 2021 and 52 in the year to September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100 in the same monitoring, while Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that violence against trans people and killings of LGBTI+ defenders had risen over the previous year.

Impunity is the recurring pattern across these cases. The 2016 murder that gave the Paola Buenrostro law its name is still unpunished, and the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights warned in 2024 that impunity for violence against trans people may reach alarming levels and demanded that investigations use methods respecting gender identity.
localsOnly:
Residents of Campeche can seek legal gender recognition through the administrative procedure created by the state's 2024 Civil Code reform, without filing suit. The procedure is a matter of state law passed by Campeche's own congress, so eligibility and processing are governed locally rather than by a federal agency.

Human Rights Watch counted Campeche among the 22 of Mexico's 32 states with such a procedure as of 31 March 2025, while noting that implementation varies widely between states; residents should expect the practical handling of a request to depend on the state office applying the reform rather than on the text of the statute alone.

Transfemicide is not an established local offence. The Paola Buenrostro law applies to Mexico City, whose attorney-general's office is obliged to publish statistics on crimes against the LGBTQ+ community; Campeche residents have no equivalent statistics obligation in the sources available here.

The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights directed its 2024 recommendations to federal and state authorities, which includes the Campeche authorities, calling on them to prevent and punish violence against trans people and to investigate LGBTI violations with methods that respect gender identity.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not state when Campeche's 2024 Civil Code reform entered into force, nor its processing times, fees, residency requirements or the documents an applicant must present. Those operational details are unresolved and not sourced here.

Whether Campeche's penal code provides for hate-crime aggravation of offences motivated by a person's gender identity is not addressed by any source in the inventory, and remains unresolved.

No source records the outcome of any individual recognition request made in Campeche under the new procedure, so the practical success rate of the administrative route is not sourced.

Whether police, prisons or health facilities in Campeche operate any trans-specific protocol or training is not covered by the inventory and is unresolved. The Beer analysis speaks to enforcement generally across Mexico but does not identify Campeche specifically.
